title: Indian National Injured as Drone Debris Kills Two at Saudi Shaybah Oil Field
excerpt: Nepali and Filipino workers were killed and Pakistani and Indian nationals injured at the Aramco-operated field on Wednesday, hours before a separate attack on Dammam's King Fahd airport killed one resident and injured eight.
body:
• Debris from an intercepted drone killed two people — Nepali and Filipino nationals — and injured two others, including an Indian national, at Saudi Arabia's Shaybah oil field on Wednesday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said.
  • The falling debris also set fire to a contractor's vehicle at the Aramco-operated field in the kingdom's southeast.
  • Hours later, an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed one resident and injured eight, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities.
  • The United States ordered non-essential diplomats and family members to leave Saudi Arabia on Wednesday as Houthi attacks on airports and oil facilities intensified.

Debris from an intercepted drone killed two workers and injured two others, including an Indian national, at an Aramco-operated oil field in southeastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said in a statement carried by NDTV and the Associated Press.

The two people killed were Nepali and Filipino nationals. The injured were Pakistani and Indian nationals, the ministry said. The falling debris sparked a fire in a contractor's vehicle at the Shaybah oil field, one of the kingdom's major producing fields. The ministry did not release the names or conditions of the casualties.

A Second Deadly Attack the Same Night

The oil field deaths were part of a wider night of attacks. Late on Wednesday, one Saudi resident was killed and eight people were injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in the Eastern Province on the Gulf coast near Bahrain and Qatar, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced early Thursday. The airport suffered material damage and flights were diverted, according to flight-tracking service Flightradar24. Authorities did not say who carried out that attack, and the Houthis had not commented on it; the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted four drone attacks in the eastern region.

Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, struck multiple times this month and shut down on October 10, was open for domestic flights on Wednesday, with Saudia and FlyNas operating, according to FlightAware data. Lufthansa and Air France have cancelled service through mid-November.

Washington Pulls Diplomats Out

Late Wednesday, the United States ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, following the series of deadly attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and rising fears of escalation. The State Department warned that the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond the immediate area. The Saudi-led coalition also reported intercepting and destroying five drones launched toward the kingdom early Wednesday, including over Madinah and the Eastern Province.

A Truce Broken, and Migrant Workers in the Line of Fire

Saudi Arabia has faced repeated attacks on its airports and oil facilities by the Iran-backed Houthis. Last month, debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed a Yemeni resident of the kingdom — the first civilian casualty since the Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi shipping and oil facilities. Earlier this month, a limited fire broke out in an administrative building at an Aramco facility in the Eastern Province.

The attacks come as renewed fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen has broken a four-year truce, marking a fresh escalation in the wider Middle East crisis. For the Gulf's large South Asian workforce — Indians form the largest expatriate community in Saudi Arabia, many of them employed in the energy and construction sectors — the casualties are a reminder that the region's oil infrastructure, and the migrant workers who run it, sit directly in the line of fire. Indian missions in the kingdom routinely advise nationals to follow local security advisories during such escalations; no official statement on the injured Indian national had been issued at the time of publication.

What to Watch

Whether the Houthis claim the Dammam airport attack, and whether strikes on energy infrastructure continue, will determine if airlines extend their cancellations beyond mid-November and whether more governments order staff out of the kingdom.
